content_html:
When a dividend stock falls below the price you paid, two things can bring the position back to even: the share price recovering and the dividends it keeps paying. This calculator estimates how long that takes if you reinvest every dividend, if you take dividends as cash, and if you rely on the share price alone.

How to use this calculator

  1. Price you paid and shares owned: together these set your cost, the amount the position needs to be worth again.
  2. Price decline: how far the stock has fallen since you bought. The current price is shown under the field.
  3. Share price growth: the yearly rate at which you assume the price recovers from here. It can be 0 or negative to test a stock that stays flat or keeps sliding.
  4. Dividend yield at today's price: the yearly dividend per share divided by the current, lower price. A falling price raises the yield if the dividend is unchanged.
  5. Dividend growth and payment frequency: how fast the dividend per share rises each year and how often it is paid.
  6. Extra investment each month: optional new money. It buys shares at the lower price but is also added to your cost, so it only helps if the price rises afterward.

How the breakeven is calculated

The calculator steps forward one month at a time for up to 50 years. Each month the share price grows at the monthly equivalent of your yearly rate. On each payment date, the dividend per share is today's price × yield, grown by the dividend growth rate and split across the payments in a year. When reinvesting, each dividend buys extra shares at that day's price. When taking cash, dividends are counted at face value and do not earn anything.

Breakeven is the first month in which the shares, plus any cash dividends, are worth at least what you paid in total. Reinvested dividends work twice: they add shares, and every added share earns its own dividends and price gains.

Worked example

With the defaults, you bought 100 shares at $100, a cost of $10,000, and the price has fallen 20% to $80, leaving a paper loss of $2,000. Assume the price grows 5% a year and the stock yields 4% at $80, with the dividend rising 3% a year and paid quarterly.

ApproachTime to break even
Reinvesting dividends2 years 8 months
Taking dividends as cash2 years 9 months
Share price alone4 years 7 months

With reinvestment you would own about 110.18 shares at breakeven, so the share price only needs to reach about $91.12 rather than the original $100. After one year the reinvested position is worth $8,736.94, or 87.4% of cost, and after two years $9,534.66, or 95.3%.

Things to keep in mind

  • A sharp drop can be a warning sign about the dividend itself. If the payout is cut, the yield you entered no longer applies, so try a lower yield or negative dividend growth.
  • Reinvesting and taking cash give similar breakeven times over short periods. The gap widens the longer recovery takes, because reinvested dividends compound.
  • Dividends in a taxable account are usually taxed in the year they are paid, even when reinvested, which slows recovery a little.
  • Breaking even on paper says nothing about whether the money would have done better elsewhere. Compare the time to recover with what a different holding might have earned.

faq.question: What is a dividend reinvestment plan (DRIP)?
faq.answer: A DRIP automatically uses each cash dividend to buy more shares of the same stock, often including fractional shares and usually without a trading commission. Many brokers let you switch it on for individual holdings.

faq.question: Why does a lower share price speed up recovery when reinvesting?
faq.answer: Each dividend buys more shares when the price is low. Those extra shares then collect their own dividends and benefit from any price recovery, so a dip can shorten the time needed to get back to even.

faq.question: Are reinvested dividends taxed?
faq.answer: In a taxable US brokerage account, dividends are generally taxable in the year they are paid whether you take them as cash or reinvest them. Each reinvestment also creates a new tax lot with its own cost basis. Dividends inside IRAs and 401(k)s are not taxed when paid.

faq.question: What happens if the stock never recovers?
faq.answer: If the price keeps falling or the yield is low, the calculator may show a breakeven of more than 50 years. That result is a signal to look again at the assumptions and at whether the holding still suits your plans.

faq.question: Does adding new money help me break even?
faq.answer: Not by itself. New money raises your total cost by the same amount it adds in value. It shortens the breakeven only when the shares it buys at the lower price later rise.
